resources.title: Water and Hydrogen Bonding: Study Guide (Biology 1.1)
resources.description: Learn how water's polarity and hydrogen bonds lead to cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling, floating ice and solvent power, and why these matter to living things.
prerequisites: Atoms, electrons and covalent bonds
Basic idea of temperature and energy (joules)
learningObjectives: Explain why the O–H bonds in water are polar and why water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Link cohesion, adhesion and surface tension to water transport in plants
Use q = mcΔT to show how water's high specific heat buffers temperature
Explain evaporative cooling, floating ice and water's solvent properties in terms of hydrogen bonding

resources.calculatorNote: Specific heat capacity of liquid water: 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Other specific heats are given where they are used
keyPoints: Oxygen pulls shared electrons harder than hydrogen, so each O–H bond is polar: O is partly negative (δ⁻), each H is partly positive (δ⁺).
A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a δ⁺ hydrogen of one molecule and a δ⁻ atom (here O) of another. Each one is weak; millions together are strong.
Hydrogen bonds explain cohesion, adhesion and surface tension, a high specific heat, a high heat of vaporization, floating ice and water's power as a solvent.
Energy for warming: q = mcΔT, with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ for water. Large c means small temperature change for a given energy.

faqs.question: Is a hydrogen bond a real chemical bond?
faqs.answer: It is an attraction between molecules (or between parts of one large molecule), not a shared pair of electrons. It is much weaker than the covalent O–H bond inside a water molecule, which is why water can boil without its molecules falling apart.

faqs.question: Do hydrogen bonds only matter for water?
faqs.answer: No. Hydrogen bonds also hold the two strands of DNA together and help proteins fold into their shapes. Water is simply the most important example in this topic.

prerequisites: Atoms, elements and chemical formulas

keyPoints: Living things cannot make atoms. They take atoms and molecules from their surroundings and rearrange them into new biological molecules.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are the most common elements in all four classes of large biological molecule.
Sulfur marks proteins (in two amino acids). Phosphorus marks nucleic acids and phospholipids (in phosphate groups). Nitrogen is in nucleic acids (in the bases) and in proteins (in every amino acid).
Because each class has its own set of elements, a radioactive sulfur or phosphorus label can show which molecules a cell is building.

faqs.question: Do carbohydrates ever contain nitrogen?
faqs.answer: Most carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. A few modified sugars carry a nitrogen-containing group; chitin, in insect skeletons and fungal cell walls, is one example. For this topic, treat carbohydrates as C, H and O.

faqs.question: Why do I need to know which elements are in which molecule?
faqs.answer: It tells you what an organism must take in from its environment, explains why a shortage of nitrate or phosphate slows growth, and lets you interpret experiments that follow labelled atoms into particular molecules.

prerequisites: Covalent bonds and the elements that make up biological molecules (Topic 1.2)

learningObjectives: Describe how dehydration synthesis joins two monomers with a covalent bond and releases the equivalent of one water molecule

keyPoints: Large biological molecules (polymers) are chains of smaller repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds.
Dehydration synthesis joins two monomers: one loses H, the other loses –OH, and together these leave as one water molecule.
Hydrolysis breaks the bond by adding water: H goes to one monomer and –OH to the other.
A straight or branched chain of n monomers has n − 1 bonds, so building it releases n − 1 water molecules and breaking it fully uses n − 1.

faqs.question: Is dehydration synthesis the same as a condensation reaction?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both names describe joining two molecules with the loss of a small molecule, here water. Many textbooks use the word condensation.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the exact structures of sugars, amino acids or nucleotides?
faqs.answer: No. The course does not assess the detailed molecular structures of specific polymers, amino acids or nucleotides. You need to describe the reactions and read diagrams of them, which is why this guide uses simple blocks.

prerequisites: Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis (Topic 1.3)

learningObjectives: Identify monosaccharides as the monomers of complex carbohydrates and give examples of each
Describe how monosaccharides are joined by covalent bonds, with the loss of water, to form disaccharides and polysaccharides

resources.calculatorNote: Atomic masses used: C = 12.011, H = 1.008, O = 15.999. Molar masses are given to 1 decimal place
keyPoints: Monosaccharides (simple sugars such as glucose) are the monomers. Polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates) are the polymers built from them.
Each link between two sugars is a covalent bond made by dehydration synthesis (one water out) and broken by hydrolysis (one water in).
Polysaccharides can be linear or branched. Shape fits function: branched glycogen releases glucose fast; linear cellulose packs into strong fibres.
Starch stores energy in plants, glycogen stores energy in animals, and cellulose builds plant cell walls. All three are made of glucose.

faqs.question: If starch and cellulose are both made of glucose, why can't humans digest cellulose?
faqs.answer: The glucose units in cellulose are joined in a different way from those in starch. Human digestive enzymes fit the links in starch but not the links in cellulose. Animals such as cows rely on microbes in their gut that make the enzymes needed.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the structure of starch or cellulose?
faqs.answer: No. The detailed molecular structure of specific carbohydrate polymers is outside the scope of the exam. You need to know the monomer, that monomers are joined by covalent bonds, whether a polymer is linear or branched, and what it does.

prerequisites: Polar and nonpolar molecules, and why nonpolar substances are hydrophobic (Topic 1.1)
Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis (Topic 1.3)
learningObjectives: Explain why most lipids are nonpolar and hydrophobic, and how their parts are put together
Tell saturated and unsaturated fatty acids apart and link the number of double bonds to kinks, packing and whether a fat is solid or liquid
Describe the jobs of fats, phospholipids, steroids and cholesterol in living things
Explain why phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer in water

resources.calculatorNote: Energy released by complete respiration: fat about 37 kJ g⁻¹; carbohydrate about 17 kJ g⁻¹. Give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Lipids are mostly carbon and hydrogen joined by nonpolar C–H bonds, so most lipids are hydrophobic. They are not polymers of repeating monomers.
A saturated fatty acid has only C–C single bonds and a straight tail. An unsaturated one has at least one C=C double bond, which kinks the tail.
More double bonds mean more kinks, looser packing and a fat that is more liquid at room temperature.
Fats store energy (about twice as much per gram as carbohydrate) and can insulate. Phospholipids form membrane bilayers. Steroids act as hormones. Cholesterol stabilises animal cell membranes.
Structure explains function: change the lipid and you change what it can do.

faqs.question: Are lipids polymers?
faqs.answer: No. Fats are made by joining fatty acids to glycerol by dehydration synthesis, but there is no long chain of repeating monomers as in starch, proteins or DNA. Lipids are grouped together because they are hydrophobic, not because they share one type of monomer.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the exact structure of cholesterol or a particular fatty acid?
faqs.answer: No. The detailed molecular structure of specific lipids is outside the scope of this course. You do need to recognise the general shapes: glycerol with fatty acid tails, a phospholipid's polar head and nonpolar tails, and the four joined rings of a steroid.

learningObjectives: Name the three parts of a nucleotide and say which sugar and which bases belong to DNA and to RNA

keyPoints: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
The information is the order of the bases. The sugar–phosphate backbone is the same all along the strand.
Every strand has a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (–OH). New nucleotides are joined by covalent bonds to the 3′ end only.
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. A pairs with T and C pairs with G by hydrogen bonds; in RNA, A pairs with U.
DNA has deoxyribose, thymine and (usually) two strands. RNA has ribose, uracil and (usually) one strand.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the chemical structure of each base?
faqs.answer: No. For this course you need the parts of a nucleotide, the 5′ and 3′ ends, the pairing rules and the DNA–RNA differences. The detailed molecular structure of individual nucleotides is outside the scope of the exam.

faqs.question: What do 5′ and 3′ actually mean?
faqs.answer: They are numbers of carbon atoms in the sugar. The phosphate is attached to carbon 5′ and the –OH group that the next nucleotide links to is on carbon 3′. The prime (′) shows that the number belongs to the sugar, not the base.

prerequisites: Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis of polymers (Topic 1.3)

learningObjectives: Describe the general structure of an amino acid and sort R groups into nonpolar, polar and ionic

keyPoints: A protein is one or more linear chains of amino acids joined by covalent peptide bonds. Each bond forms between a carboxyl group and the next amine group, and releases one water molecule.
Every amino acid has the same core (central carbon, H, amine group, carboxyl group) plus a variable R group that is nonpolar, polar or ionic.
Primary structure is the sequence. Secondary structure (α-helices, β-pleated sheets) comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.
Tertiary structure comes from R-group interactions: hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic interactions and disulfide bridges. Quaternary structure is two or more chains fitting together.
The sequence decides the shape, and the shape decides the function. One changed amino acid can be enough to change both.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the structures of all the amino acids?
faqs.answer: No. You need the general structure that every amino acid shares and the three types of R group. The course framework places the detailed structures of individual amino acids outside the exam.

faqs.question: Does every protein have quaternary structure?
faqs.answer: No. Only proteins made of two or more polypeptide chains have quaternary structure. A protein made of a single chain has three levels of structure.

faqs.question: If f(c) is defined, can there still be a discontinuity at c?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the limit at c exists but is different from f(c), the discontinuity is removable. If the one-sided limits are finite but different, it is a jump, whatever f(c) is.

faqs.question: Does a zero in the denominator always mean a vertical asymptote?
faqs.answer: No. If the factor that makes the denominator zero cancels with the numerator, the graph has a hole instead. Factor first, then decide.

faqs.question: Is 1/x a continuous function?
faqs.answer: It is continuous at every point of its domain, so it is continuous on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞). It is not continuous on any interval that contains 0, such as [−1, 1], because it is not defined at 0.

faqs.question: Do I have to check every point of an interval one by one?
faqs.answer: No. The family facts cover all the points inside each piece at once. You only test special points: where a piece changes, where the formula is undefined, and the endpoints of the interval you were asked about.

faqs.question: Why can I not remove a jump by choosing a better value of f(c)?
faqs.answer: At a jump the left-hand and right-hand limits are different numbers. One value of f(c) cannot equal both, so the limit does not exist and no choice of f(c) makes f continuous.

faqs.question: Do I need to worry about which piece contains the boundary point?
faqs.answer: Yes. The piece with ≤ or ≥ at the boundary gives f(c). For continuity all three values must agree, so in practice you set the two expressions equal at c, and f(c) then matches automatically.

faqs.question: If I write lim (x → 2) f(x) = ∞, does the limit exist?
faqs.answer: No. The limit does not exist as a real number. Writing = ∞ gives extra information: it says why it fails to exist (the values grow without bound and are all positive).

faqs.question: Does a vertical asymptote need both one-sided limits to be infinite?
faqs.answer: No. One infinite one-sided limit is enough. For example, e^(1/x) → +∞ as x → 0 from the right but → 0 from the left, and x = 0 is still a vertical asymptote.

faqs.question: Can a graph cross its horizontal asymptote?
faqs.answer: Yes. A horizontal asymptote only describes what happens far to the left or far to the right. In the middle, the graph can cross it, even many times.

faqs.question: Is ∞ a number I can substitute?

faqs.question: Why are particle numbers so large?
faqs.answer: Atoms are tiny: one carbon atom has a mass of about 2 × 10⁻²³ g. Any sample you can weigh therefore holds roughly 10²² particles or more.

faqs.question: Why do I assume a 100 g sample when I am given percentages?
faqs.answer: It makes each percentage equal to a mass in grams. 40.0% carbon becomes 40.0 g of carbon. Any sample size gives the same ratio, so 100 g is just the easiest choice.

faqs.question: Does the law of definite proportions work for mixtures?
faqs.answer: No. A mixture such as salt water can have any proportion of its parts. The law applies only to a pure compound. Mixtures are the subject of Topic 1.4.

faqs.answer: No. Salt dissolved in water looks the same everywhere but contains two types of particle. Only the particle-level make-up, or data such as elemental analysis, tells you whether a sample is pure.

faqs.question: Is a PES peak the same as an ionization energy?

faqs.question: What is the difference between electron affinity and electronegativity?
faqs.answer: Electron affinity is a measured energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron. Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a covalent bond, on a scale with no unit.

faqs.question: Is scarcity the same as a shortage?
faqs.answer: No. Scarcity is permanent and affects every economy: there are never enough resources for everything people want. A shortage is usually temporary and affects one market: buyers want more of a good than sellers offer at the current price.

faqs.question: Does unemployment shift the PPC inward?
faqs.answer: No. Unemployed workers still exist, so the economy's capacity is unchanged. Extra unemployment, such as in a recession, puts the economy at a point inside the PPC. The curve shifts inward only if the economy actually loses resources or productivity.

faqs.question: Why is the PPC usually drawn bowed outward?
faqs.answer: Because resources are not equally good at producing both goods. As an economy makes more of one good, it has to move resources that are less and less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.

faqs.question: Is a country with an absolute advantage in both goods better off not trading?
faqs.answer: No. It still gains by specialising in the good where its opportunity cost is lower and buying the other good at terms of trade that are cheaper than its own opportunity cost.

A straight PPC means constant opportunity cost; a PPC bowed outward means increasing opportunity cost.
More or better resources, or better technology, shift the PPC outward (growth). Re-employing idle resources only moves a point towards the curve.

faqs.question: Is a point inside the PPC impossible?
faqs.answer: No. A point inside is easy to reach; it is simply wasteful. The economy could have more of at least one good without giving up any of the other.

faqs.question: Why do we only use two goods?
faqs.answer: Two goods let us draw the trade-off on a flat graph. The second good can stand for 'everything else', so the model still says something about a real economy.

faqs.question: Can one country have a comparative advantage in both goods?
faqs.answer: No. With two goods and two producers, if one has the lower opportunity cost for one good, the other must have the lower opportunity cost for the second good. If the costs are equal, neither has a comparative advantage.

faqs.question: Is an implicit cost a real cost if no money changes hands?

faqs.question: Do all the atoms in a gas at one temperature move at the same speed?

faqs.question: Do I need to know the equation of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve?

faqs.question: When should I use n and R, and when N and k_B?

faqs.question: Does a real gas obey PV = nRT?
faqs.answer: Approximately, when the gas is at low pressure and well above the temperature at which it condenses. Then the atoms are far apart and the model's assumptions are reasonable. At high pressure or near condensation, real gases deviate from the model.

faqs.question: Is heat the same as temperature?
faqs.answer: No. Temperature describes the average kinetic energy of the atoms in a system. Heating is a transfer of energy caused by a temperature difference. A system has a temperature; it does not contain heat.

faqs.question: Why does a metal bench feel colder than a wooden one at the same temperature?
faqs.answer: Both are at the same temperature, below your skin temperature. Metal conducts energy away from your hand much faster than wood, so your skin cools faster and you feel cold. Your hand senses the rate of energy loss, not the bench's temperature.

faqs.question: Does a refrigerator break the second law?

faqs.question: Is "data" singular or plural?
faqs.answer: Strictly, "data" is plural. One piece of information about one item or individual is a datum. A whole collection of data is a data set.

faqs.question: What is the difference between N and n?
faqs.answer: Capital N is the population size: how many items or individuals the question is about. Lower-case n is the sample size: how many you actually collected data from. For a sample, n is smaller than N.

faqs.question: Does the population have to be people?
faqs.answer: No. A population can be apples in an orchard, chargers made in a week, days in a year or photos on a website. It is whatever set of items or individuals the question is about.

faqs.question: Is a census an observational study?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. A census is about who is measured (everyone in the population). Observational study versus experiment is about how the data are produced (recorded or imposed). If no treatment is imposed, a census is an observational study of the whole population.

faqs.question: Do I need to carry out a hypothesis test or confidence interval in this topic?
faqs.answer: No. Here you only need to recognise what kind of analysis an investigative question asks for. You will build confidence intervals and carry out tests later in the course, starting in Unit 3.

faqs.question: Are 'factor' and 'explanatory variable' the same thing?
faqs.answer: Yes. In an experiment, a factor is an explanatory variable whose levels the researcher imposes. Each level, or each combination of levels when there is more than one factor, is a treatment.

keyPoints: A random sample uses a chance process, such as a random number generator, to choose every individual.
Without replacement, an individual can be chosen only once. With replacement, it goes back and could be chosen again.
Simple random sample (SRS): every possible sample of size n has the same chance of being chosen.
Stratified: take an SRS from every stratum (similar individuals). Cluster: pick whole clusters at random and measure everyone in them.
Systematic: a random starting point, then every k-th individual on the list.
The best method depends on the question, the groups in the population and the cost of reaching people.

faqs.question: Is a stratified random sample a simple random sample?
faqs.answer: No. In a stratified sample some samples of size n can never happen, for example a sample taken entirely from one stratum. In an SRS every sample of size n is possible and equally likely.

faqs.question: How do I remember the difference between strata and clusters?
faqs.answer: Strata are similar inside and different from each other; you sample from every stratum. Clusters are each a small copy of the population; you choose some clusters and measure everyone in them.

faqs.question: What is the difference between voluntary response bias and nonresponse bias?
faqs.answer: In voluntary response, people choose themselves to be in the sample. In nonresponse, the researcher chose the people (often at random), but some of them did not reply. Ask: who decided who is in the sample?

faqs.question: If a sample is chosen at random, can it still be biased?
faqs.answer: Yes. Random selection protects against bias in who is chosen, but not against nonresponse, response bias, or undercoverage caused by an incomplete list.

faqs.question: Does a biased method always give a wrong answer?
faqs.answer: Not every time. Bias describes what happens on average over many samples taken the same way. One sample may land close to the parameter by chance, but the method still tends to miss in one direction.

faqs.question: Is random assignment the same as random sampling?
faqs.answer: No. Random sampling chooses who is in the study, which lets you generalise to the population. Random assignment decides which treatment each unit gets, which lets you draw a cause-and-effect conclusion. An experiment can have one, both or neither.

faqs.question: Does every experiment need a placebo?
faqs.answer: No. You need a placebo when knowing that you received a treatment could change the response, as with people taking a pill. A control group can also be the current standard treatment, or no treatment at all.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a bar chart and a histogram?
faqs.answer: A bar chart shows a categorical variable: each bar is a category, the bars have gaps between them, and the order of the categories can be changed. A histogram (Topic 1.5) shows a quantitative variable: each bar is an interval of numbers, the bars touch, and the order is fixed by the number line.

faqs.question: Should my bar chart show counts or relative frequencies?
faqs.answer: For one group, either is fine: the bars have the same shape and only the scale on the axis changes. To compare groups of different sizes, use relative frequencies so that each group is measured out of 1.

faqs.question: A value sits exactly on the edge between two bins. Which bin does it go in?
faqs.answer: Choose one rule and use it for every bin. This guide uses bins such as 30 ≤ x < 45, so a value of 45 goes in the next bin, 45 to under 60. Label the bins so the reader can see your rule.

faqs.question: How many bins should a histogram have?
faqs.answer: There is no single correct number. A small data set needs only a few bins; a large one can use more. Try two widths. If the shape changes a lot, choose the one that shows the pattern without lots of empty or one-value bars, and say which width you used.

faqs.question: Is a histogram the same as a bar chart?
faqs.answer: No. A bar chart shows a categorical variable, so its bars are separate and their order can be changed. A histogram shows a quantitative variable on a number line, so its bins are in numerical order and the bars touch.

faqs.question: How do I decide if a distribution is skewed or approximately symmetric?
faqs.answer: Find the main peak and compare the two sides. If one tail stretches much further than the other, the distribution is skewed towards the longer tail. If the two halves are roughly mirror images, call it approximately symmetric. Real data are never perfectly symmetric, so use the word 'approximately'.

faqs.question: Do I need a formula to call a value an outlier in this topic?
faqs.answer: Not yet. In this topic you judge by eye whether a value is unusually far from the rest and call it a possible outlier. Topic 1.7 adds two numerical rules (the 1.5 × IQR rule and the 2-standard-deviation rule).

faqs.question: Why does the sample standard deviation divide by n − 1 and not n?
faqs.answer: The deviations are measured from x̄, which is itself calculated from the same data, so they are slightly too small on average. Dividing by n − 1 corrects for this. The course uses s with n − 1 throughout; on a calculator this is Sx.

faqs.question: My calculator gives a different Q1 from my textbook. Which is right?
faqs.answer: Several quartile methods exist. This guide uses the method most graphing calculators use: split the ordered data at the median and, when n is odd, leave the median out of both halves. Show your method and the answer will be clear.

faqs.question: Can I tell the shape of a distribution from its mean and median alone?
